client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away six months ago from cancer. Everything just feels kind of gray and empty, like I go through the motions every day but nothing actually feels meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you're carrying — the loss of your partner, the emptiness, the sense of just going through the motions — is one of the heaviest things a person can experience, and it makes complete sense that things feel gray right now. I also notice there's something quietly brave in showing up here even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that doubt is welcome here too. Can you tell me a little more about what a typical day looks like for you these days?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: A typical day is pretty bleak, honestly. I wake up and for just a second I forget, and then it all comes back and there's this heavy feeling in my chest that just sits there all day. I go to work, I come home, I eat something, I watch TV without really watching it, and then I go to bed and do it all again.
therapist: That moment every morning when it all comes rushing back sounds absolutely exhausting — like you have to lose him again and again, every single day. The way you describe moving through your routine, eating, watching TV without really watching — it sounds less like living and more like waiting for the day to be over. What do you think gets you through to the next morning, even on the hardest days?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I'm not sure anything "gets me through" in any meaningful way — I just kind of... keep existing, I guess. Maybe habit, or maybe I feel like I owe it to him somehow to not just fall apart completely. But some nights I lie there and I genuinely don't know what I'm doing any of this for anymore.
therapist: That sense of "I owe it to him not to fall apart" is such a tender thing — it speaks to how much love is still alive in you, even in the middle of all this pain. I want to gently check in though, because when you say you don't know what you're doing any of this for anymore, I want to make sure I understand — are you having any thoughts of not wanting to be here, or of harming yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: No, it's not like that — I'm not thinking about hurting myself or anything. It's more like I just feel... purposeless, like the future used to make sense because he was in it, and now I can't picture what it's supposed to look like without him. It's less about not wanting to be here and more about not knowing how to be here in a way that feels real again.
therapist: That distinction you're making — not wanting to disappear, but not knowing how to exist in a way that feels real — is really important, and it makes a lot of sense when someone who was so central to your sense of future is suddenly gone. I notice you said that quite quickly, like there's a lot pressing up against those words — is there something about trying to imagine that future that feels particularly painful or overwhelming right now? You don't have to have any answers, I'm just curious what comes up when you try.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: When I try to picture the future, it's just... blank. Like there's literally nothing there, no images, no feelings, just this void where everything used to be. We had plans, you know, things we were going to do together, places we were going to go, and now those things feel almost cruel to think about because they're just reminders of what's never going to happen.
therapist: The way you describe those plans — places you were going to go, things you were going to do — it sounds like they've transformed from something that once brought joy into something that now feels almost like a wound. There's something so tender in your voice when you talk about this, like you're holding it very carefully, almost protecting yourself from the full weight of it. I'm wondering, are there any of those plans or dreams that feel especially hard to let go of, one that carries the most of him?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: We were supposed to go to Portugal together — it was this whole thing we'd been planning for two years, saving up, looking at little towns to stay in, bookmarking restaurants. He got diagnosed before we ever got to go, and now I have this whole folder on my laptop of places we picked out together that I can't bring myself to open or delete. It just sits there, and I don't know what to do with it.
therapist: That folder sounds like it holds so much — two years of hope and excitement and the future you were building together, all still sitting there, waiting. The way you're describing it, I can hear something very quiet and careful in how you're holding this, like maybe the words don't quite capture how much that folder actually means to you. I'm wondering if part of what makes it so impossible to open or delete is that doing either one feels like it would force a decision about what his memory — and that dream — gets to mean going forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think that's exactly it — opening it feels like I'm moving toward something, and deleting it feels like I'm erasing him, and I can't do either one. It's like as long as it just sits there untouched, I don't have to make any kind of statement about what any of it means now. I know that probably sounds like I'm just avoiding things, but it genuinely feels like the only option that doesn't hurt in an unbearable way.
therapist: What you're describing isn't avoidance in any simple or weak sense — it's actually a very human way of protecting something precious when every available path feels like a kind of loss. That folder isn't just files; it's a space where the two of you still exist together, and leaving it untouched is its own form of honoring that. I'm curious — when you imagine a version of the future where that folder still exists but somehow feels less like a trap, what would need to be different for that to be possible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I honestly don't know what would need to be different — that's kind of the problem, right? Like I can't even imagine a version of myself that could look at that folder and feel something other than grief and guilt. And I think part of me worries that if it ever did feel okay to open it, that would mean I'd somehow gotten over him, and I don't want to get over him.
therapist: What you just said carries so much — this fear that healing somehow means betrayal, that feeling okay would mean leaving him behind. But I notice that even as you're saying these words, there's something that feels almost rushed, like maybe there's more emotion pressing underneath than you're quite letting out right now. I want to gently offer this: what if "getting over him" isn't actually what healing looks like — what if it's possible to carry him with you *into* the future, rather than having to choose between grief and moving forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That sounds nice in theory, but I'm not sure I actually know what that means in practice — like, what does "carrying him with you" actually look like day to day? Because right now it just feels like carrying a weight, not carrying him, if that makes sense. I want to believe there's a version of this that doesn't feel like either betrayal or just endless pain, but I can't see how to get there from where I am right now.
therapist: That distinction you just made — carrying a weight versus carrying *him* — is really profound, and I think it points to something important about where you are right now. The weight is what grief feels like before meaning has had a chance to form around it, and you're still very much in that raw place. I wonder if we could start very small — not with the folder, not with Portugal, but just with one thing, however tiny, that was *him* in a way that still feels like warmth rather than only pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: There's this one thing — he used to make this really specific cup of coffee on Sunday mornings, with too much sugar and a little bit of cinnamon, and sometimes when I smell cinnamon now I feel both close to him and completely destroyed at the same time. I guess that's maybe what you mean, but I'm not sure sitting with that feeling is something I can do on purpose — it usually just hits me and I try to get through it as fast as possible.
therapist: That image — the too much sugar, the cinnamon, the Sunday mornings — that's not just a memory, that's *him*, something specific and irreplaceable that only you two shared. I notice as you described it your voice became very soft, almost like you were handling something fragile, and I wonder if part of rushing through those moments when cinnamon hits you is a way of protecting yourself from how much tenderness is actually in there alongside the pain. What if, just as an idea, the goal wasn't to sit in it longer but simply to let yourself notice — even for one breath — that the closeness and the grief are arriving together because they come from the same love?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
